concepts.name: Scientific method
concepts.statement: Chemistry is a science based on observation and experimentation, and there is no single route from a question to an answer. What every route has in common is that it rests on experiments that can be repeated, so the path from question and observation to hypothesis, and from hypothesis through testing to law or theory, is the method the whole of the book argues by.

concepts.name: Telling a hypothesis, law and theory apart
concepts.statement: Outside science these three words are loose; inside it they are precise. A hypothesis is a tentative explanation that guides the gathering of information, a law summarizes a vast number of observations and predicts, and a theory is a well-substantiated explanation that has survived a large body of data. Knowing which of the three a statement is tells you how much weight it carries.

concepts.name: Domains of chemistry
concepts.statement: Chemists describe matter in three domains at once: the macroscopic, which you can see and touch; the microscopic, which is mostly imagined; and the symbolic, the formulas and equations that stand for either. One challenge of learning chemistry is that the same symbol can stand for a thing in one domain or the other, and one pleasure is explaining what you observe by what you must imagine.

concepts.name: Chemistry
concepts.statement: Chemistry is the study of the composition, properties, and interactions of matter.

concepts.name: Hypothesis
concepts.statement: A hypothesis is a tentative explanation of observations that acts as a guide for gathering and checking information.

concepts.name: Law
concepts.statement: A law is a statement that summarizes a vast number of experimental observations and describes or predicts some aspect of the natural world.

concepts.name: Theory
concepts.statement: A theory is a well-substantiated, comprehensive, testable explanation of a particular aspect of nature.

concepts.name: Macroscopic domain
concepts.statement: The macroscopic domain is the realm of everyday things that are large enough to sense directly by human sight and touch.

concepts.name: Microscopic domain
concepts.statement: The microscopic domain is the realm of things that are much too small to be sensed directly.

concepts.name: Symbolic domain
concepts.statement: The symbolic domain is the specialized language used to represent components of the macroscopic and microscopic domains, such as chemical symbols, chemical formulas, chemical equations, graphs, drawings, and calculations.

concepts.name: Matter
concepts.statement: Matter is anything that occupies space and has mass. A gas is as much matter as a solid is, even though you can neither see nor hold it.

concepts.name: States of matter
concepts.statement: A solid is rigid and keeps its shape, a liquid flows and keeps its volume, and a gas takes both the shape and the volume of its container; a plasma is a gas carrying enough charged particles to behave unlike one. These are the states the book will move a substance between for the rest of the chapters, so the properties that tell them apart come first.

concepts.name: Mass versus weight
concepts.statement: The mass of an object measures the amount of matter in it and does not change; weight is the force gravity exerts on it and changes with the gravity it sits in. An astronaut's mass is the same on the moon as on the earth while her weight is one sixth of it, so it is mass, not weight, that says how much matter is present.

concepts.name: Law of conservation of matter
concepts.statement: There is no detectable change in the total quantity of matter when matter converts from one type to another or changes among the solid, liquid and gaseous states. Every balanced equation and every mass calculation of the later chapters rests on this law, and a mass that seems to vanish has gone somewhere nobody weighed.

concepts.name: Elements and compounds
concepts.statement: A pure substance has a constant composition. An element cannot be broken down into anything simpler by a chemical change; a compound is made of two or more elements and can be broken down into them. The properties of combined elements are nothing like their properties uncombined, which is why sodium and chlorine make table salt.

concepts.name: Homogeneous and heterogeneous mixtures
concepts.statement: A mixture holds two or more kinds of matter in amounts that can vary and can be separated again by physical means. A heterogeneous mixture varies in composition from point to point, as salad dressing does; a homogeneous mixture, also called a solution, is the same throughout, as a sports drink is. The difference is what a sample taken from one place tells about the rest.

concepts.name: Classifying a sample of matter
concepts.statement: Given a sample, the reader should be able to place it: constant composition or not, uniform or not, simplifiable by a chemical change or not. Two questions sort every sample into an element, a compound, a homogeneous mixture or a heterogeneous mixture, and the classification decides what can be done with the sample.

concepts.name: Atoms and molecules
concepts.statement: An atom is the smallest particle of an element that keeps the properties of that element and can enter into a chemical combination; a molecule is two or more atoms joined by chemical bonds and moving about as a unit. Atoms are far too small and too light to imagine directly, and the whole microscopic domain of the book is built out of them.

concepts.name: Mass
concepts.statement: The mass of an object is a measure of the amount of matter in it, and it does not change with where the object is.

concepts.name: Weight
concepts.statement: The weight of an object is the force that gravity exerts on it, so it changes with the gravity the object is in.

concepts.name: Gas
concepts.statement: A gas is a state of matter that has neither definite volume nor shape.

concepts.name: Liquid
concepts.statement: A liquid is a state of matter that has a definite volume but indefinite shape.

concepts.name: Solid
concepts.statement: A solid is a state of matter that is rigid, has a definite shape, and has a fairly constant volume.

concepts.name: Plasma
concepts.statement: A plasma is a gaseous state of matter containing a large number of electrically charged atoms and/or molecules.

concepts.name: Pure substance
concepts.statement: A pure substance is a homogeneous substance that has a constant composition.

concepts.name: Element
concepts.statement: An element is a substance composed of a single type of atom, one that cannot be decomposed by a chemical change.

concepts.name: Compound
concepts.statement: A compound is a pure substance that can be decomposed into two or more elements.

concepts.name: Mixture
concepts.statement: A mixture is matter that can be separated into its components by physical means.

concepts.name: Heterogeneous mixture
concepts.statement: A heterogeneous mixture is a combination of substances with a composition that varies from point to point.

concepts.name: Homogeneous mixture
concepts.statement: A homogeneous mixture, also called a solution, is a combination of substances with a composition that is uniform throughout.

concepts.name: Atom
concepts.statement: An atom is the smallest particle of an element that can enter into a chemical combination.

concepts.name: Molecule
concepts.statement: A molecule is a bonded collection of two or more atoms of the same or different elements.

concepts.name: Physical properties
concepts.statement: A physical property is a characteristic of matter that is not associated with a change in its chemical composition: density, color, hardness, melting and boiling point, electrical conductivity. Some can be observed without changing the matter at all, and others only while it is changing state, but in neither case does the substance become a different substance.

concepts.name: Chemical properties
concepts.statement: A chemical property is the ability of a substance to change into another kind of matter, or its inability to do so. Flammability, toxicity, acidity and reactivity are chemical properties, and unlike a physical property, one cannot be observed without the substance in question becoming something else.

concepts.name: Physical and chemical change
concepts.statement: A physical change alters the state, form or properties of matter and leaves its chemical identity alone; a chemical change always produces one or more kinds of matter that were not there before. Wax melting and sugar dissolving are the first; rust forming and a match burning are the second, and the test is whether what is left is the same substance.

concepts.name: Classifying a change
concepts.statement: To decide which kind of change a described event is, ask one question: is the matter left afterward the same kind of matter as the matter there before? A gas that expands has changed physically; a gas that has burned has not.

concepts.name: Extensive and intensive properties
concepts.statement: An extensive property depends on how much matter is present and is directly proportional to it; an intensive property does not. Mass and volume are extensive, temperature and density intensive, and the distinction matters because an intensive property identifies a substance while an extensive one only measures a sample of it.

concepts.name: Physical change
concepts.statement: A physical change is a change in the state or properties of matter that does not involve a change in its chemical composition.

concepts.name: Chemical change
concepts.statement: A chemical change is a change producing a different kind of matter from the original kind of matter.

concepts.name: Extensive property
concepts.statement: An extensive property is a property of a substance that depends on the amount of the substance.

concepts.name: Intensive property
concepts.statement: An intensive property is a property of a substance that is independent of the amount of the substance.

concepts.name: Parts of a measurement
concepts.statement: Every measurement provides three kinds of information: a number, a unit that says what the number is compared against, and an uncertainty. You write down the number and the unit and carry the uncertainty implicitly. A quantity missing any of the three is at best confusing: a dose of one hundred without its unit can be a treatment or a lethal amount.

concepts.name: Writing a measurement in scientific notation
concepts.statement: A number in a measurement can be written in decimal form or in scientific notation, and for the very large and the very small the second is the only readable one. The mass of a mosquito is more usefully written as 2.5 x 10 to the minus 6 kilograms than as a string of zeros, and the notation will also be what settles how many digits of a measurement are meant.

concepts.name: SI base units
concepts.statement: Seven fundamental properties have units fixed by international agreement, and every other unit in the book is derived from them. Knowing that the meter, the kilogram, the second, the kelvin, the ampere, the mole and the candela are the base units is what makes a unit conversion a matter of bookkeeping rather than of memory.

concepts.name: Using the SI prefixes
concepts.statement: Fractions and multiples of an SI unit are always powers of ten, and each power has a prefix and a symbol. A kilometer is a thousand meters and a microliter is a millionth of a liter, so a reader who knows the prefixes can move a measurement up and down the scale without arithmetic.

concepts.name: Derived units
concepts.statement: Many units are built out of the base units rather than agreed separately: a volume is a length cubed, and a density is a mass divided by a volume. Seeing a unit as the product and quotient of base units is what lets the reader check that a calculation has produced the kind of quantity it was meant to.

concepts.name: Volume and its units
concepts.statement: Volume is the amount of space an object occupies, and its standard unit is the cubic meter, a cube one meter on an edge. The cubic decimeter is a liter and the cubic centimeter is a milliliter, so the units a chemist actually works in are nested inside the standard one by factors of a thousand.

concepts.name: Density
concepts.statement: The density of a substance is the ratio of the mass of a sample to its volume. It is an intensive property, so it identifies a substance rather than a sample: a brick of gold and a brick of lead of the same size do not have the same mass.

concepts.name: Measuring volume by displacement
concepts.statement: A cube's volume can be calculated from its edge, but most objects are not cubes. Lowering an object into a partly filled graduated cylinder raises the water by exactly the object's volume, which turns an irregular shape into a subtraction and makes the density of anything that sinks measurable with a balance and a cylinder.

concepts.name: Unit
concepts.statement: A unit is a standard of comparison for measurements; the number of a measured quantity says how many of its unit the quantity holds.

concepts.name: Length
concepts.statement: Length is the measure of one dimension of an object, and its SI unit is the meter.

concepts.name: Time
concepts.statement: Time is measured in the SI base unit of time, the second.

concepts.name: Temperature
concepts.statement: Temperature is an intensive property representing the hotness or coldness of matter, and its SI unit is the kelvin.

concepts.name: SI units
concepts.statement: SI units are the standards fixed by international agreement in the International System of Units (Le Système International d’Unités).

concepts.name: Meter
concepts.statement: The meter (m) is the standard metric and SI unit of length; 1 m is approximately 1.094 yards.

concepts.name: Kilogram
concepts.statement: The kilogram (kg) is the standard SI unit of mass.

concepts.name: Second
concepts.statement: The second (s) is the SI unit of time.

concepts.name: Kelvin
concepts.statement: The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of temperature; 273.15 K equals 0 °C.

concepts.name: Degree Celsius
concepts.statement: The degree Celsius (°C) is a unit of temperature; water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C on this scale.

concepts.name: Cubic meter
concepts.statement: The cubic meter (m³) is the SI unit of volume, the volume of a cube with an edge length of exactly 1 m.

concepts.name: Cubic centimeter
concepts.statement: The cubic centimeter (cm³ or cc) is the volume of a cube with an edge length of exactly 1 cm.

concepts.name: Liter
concepts.statement: The liter (L), also called the cubic decimeter, is a unit of volume; 1 L equals 1,000 cm³.

concepts.name: Milliliter
concepts.statement: The milliliter (mL) is 1/1,000 of a liter and equals 1 cm³.

concepts.name: Exact and uncertain numbers
concepts.statement: Counting is the only measurement free of uncertainty, and numbers fixed by definition are exact in the same way: a foot is exactly twelve inches and an inch exactly 2.54 centimeters. Every other quantity is uncertain to some extent, and knowing which numbers in a calculation are exact decides which of them can limit the answer.

concepts.name: Every measurement carries an uncertainty
concepts.statement: A measurement is read as far as the instrument allows and then one digit further, and that last digit is an estimate. A scale with one milliliter divisions can be read to a tenth of a milliliter, and a balance that reads 6.72 grams is saying the mass lies between 6.71 and 6.73, so uncertainty is a property of the instrument and the reader together, not a mistake.

concepts.name: Significant figures
concepts.statement: All of the digits in a measurement, including the uncertain last one, are its significant figures, and their number is how a written quantity says how certain it is. A result is properly reported when its significant digits represent the certainty of the process that produced it, and no better.

concepts.name: Counting significant figures
concepts.statement: The rule is to start at the first nonzero digit on the left and count every digit to its right, and the only difficulty is the zeros. A captive zero results from measurement and is always significant, a leading zero only locates the decimal point and never is, and a trailing zero to the left of the decimal point is ambiguous unless the number is written in scientific notation.

concepts.name: Rounding to a given number of digits
concepts.statement: A digit to be dropped that is less than five rounds down, and one greater than five rounds up. When the dropped digit is a five with nothing but zeros after it, round the retained digit to whichever value is even. This rule from statistics keeps the rounding from leaning one way over many calculations.

concepts.name: Carrying significant figures through a calculation
concepts.statement: A result calculated from measurements is at least as uncertain as the measurements it came from, so the answer has to be rounded rather than copied off the calculator. A sum or difference is rounded to the decimal place of the least precise term, and a product or quotient to the number of significant figures of the least certain factor.

concepts.name: Accuracy and precision
concepts.statement: Measurements are precise when repeating them gives very similar results and accurate when they fall close to the true or accepted value, and the two are independent. A dispenser can be precise and consistently wrong, or accurate on average and scattered, and only one that is both is working.

concepts.name: Exact number
concepts.statement: An exact number is a number derived by counting or by definition.

concepts.name: Uncertainty
concepts.statement: The uncertainty of a measurement is an estimate of the amount by which it differs from the true value.

concepts.name: Rounding
concepts.statement: Rounding is the procedure used to ensure that calculated results properly reflect the uncertainty in the measurements used in the calculation.

concepts.name: Accuracy
concepts.statement: Accuracy is how closely a measurement aligns with a correct value.

concepts.name: Precision
concepts.statement: Precision is how closely a measurement matches the same measurement when repeated.

concepts.name: Dimensional analysis
concepts.statement: The units of quantities must be subjected to the same mathematical operations as their numbers. That one premise is what lets a reader divide a distance by a time and get a speed, and it is also what lets the reader check a calculation by looking only at the units, since a wrong arrangement of factors gives a unit nobody wanted.

forms.condition: an average speed, computed from a measured distance and the time taken to cover it

concepts.name: Unit conversion factor
concepts.statement: A ratio of two equivalent quantities in different units equals one, so multiplying by it changes a quantity's units without changing the quantity. The ratio can go either way up, so you choose the arrangement that cancels the unit you want gone and leaves the one you want.

concepts.name: Converting units
concepts.statement: Multiplying by one conversion factor after another, each oriented so that the unwanted unit cancels, converts a measurement through as many steps as it takes. It is the most-used skill of the chapter, and it works the same whether the conversion is between two metric units, between metric and customary units, or between units of an area or a volume.

concepts.name: Computing with mixed units
concepts.statement: Beyond a simple conversion, the factor-label method solves a problem in which the quantity wanted is computed from two or more measured ones given in the wrong units. All the factors are arranged in one line so that the labels cancel and combine into the unit of the answer, and the arithmetic is done once at the end.

concepts.name: Linear versus proportional scales
concepts.statement: Most units of a property are directly proportional to one another and a single conversion factor moves between them. The Celsius and Fahrenheit scales do not share a zero, so the relation between them is a line with an intercept rather than a line through the origin, and converting between them takes both a slope and an offset.

concepts.name: Temperature scales
concepts.statement: You fix a temperature scale by choosing reference temperatures and dividing the space between them. Celsius puts the freezing and boiling of water at 0 and 100, Fahrenheit at 32 and 212. Kelvin is absolute: its zero is the lowest temperature theoretically achievable, and its unit carries no degree symbol.

concepts.name: Converting between Celsius and Fahrenheit
concepts.statement: The Fahrenheit temperature is nine fifths of the Celsius temperature plus thirty-two, and the relation rearranges to give the Celsius temperature from the Fahrenheit one. Both forms are on the book's key equation list, and they are the conversion a reader meets outside the laboratory more often than any other.

concepts.name: Converting between Celsius and kelvin
concepts.statement: A kelvin and a Celsius degree are the same size, so the two scales differ only by where their zeros sit: adding 273.15 to a Celsius temperature gives the kelvin temperature and subtracting it goes back. The 273.15 was determined experimentally and is not exact, which matters when the result is rounded.

concepts.name: Degree Fahrenheit
concepts.statement: The degree Fahrenheit (°F) is a unit of temperature; water freezes at 32 °F and boils at 212 °F on this scale.
